one_liner: Toy benchmark: hand-written AVX2/FMA GNU-as i-k-j double matmul beating a GCC -O3 build restricted to SSE2.
what_it_does: Two standalone Linux x86-64 programs (matrix_benchmark.c and matrix_benchmark_gas.s) load two binary matrices, multiply them 1,000 times with the same i-k-j triple loop, time the loop and write the result; gen_matrix.c makes random inputs and verify.py compares outputs with a 1e-12 relative tolerance. It is a benchmark, not a library: the assembly matrix_mul is a local label taking a {int rows; int cols; double *data} struct, with no exported API or header.
how_it_is_fast: The assembly inner loop broadcasts A[i][k] into a YMM register (vbroadcastsd) and updates eight doubles of the C row per iteration with two 256-bit vfmadd231pd, 2x unrolled; the C build has no -march/-mavx2/-mfma, so GCC can only emit 2-wide SSE2 mulpd plus addpd. The gain therefore comes from vector width and FMA, not from scheduling the compiler could not do; neither side uses register or cache blocking, so every k step re-loads and re-stores the C row and all of B is streamed once per output row.
when_to_use: As a readable teaching example of an AVX2/FMA broadcast-and-FMA inner loop in GNU as Intel syntax, including the System V calling details it had to fix (clock_gettime argument order, varargs stack order, vzeroupper).
As a starting point for a classroom demonstration of compiler flags: rebuild matrix_benchmark.c with -O3 -march=x86-64-v3 (or -mavx2 -mfma) and compare against the shipped assembly.
Only on x86-64 Linux CPUs with AVX2 and FMA (Haswell or Zen 1 and later), with square-ish matrices whose column count is a multiple of 8.
when_not_to_use: Any real dense matrix multiply: the kernel has no register or cache blocking, reaching about 4.4 GFLOP/s on 200x200 doubles; use a BLAS such as BLIS or OpenBLAS (wave 8 entries) instead.
As evidence that hand-written assembly beats GCC: the C side was compiled for baseline x86-64 (SSE2, no FMA) and an AVX2/FMA build of the same C loop was never measured.
Matrices whose B has fewer than 8 columns: the .scalar_only path jumps past `xor edx, edx`, so the column counter is uninitialised and results are wrong or the loop indexes out of bounds.

Column counts that are not a multiple of 8 when bit-reproducibility or speed matters: the tail uses legacy-SSE mulsd/addsd (no FMA, non-VEX) after 256-bit code, mixing roundings and risking SSE/AVX transition stalls.
Non-Linux, non-x86-64 or pre-AVX2 targets: there is no CPU dispatch or fallback, and the file is GNU as syntax only.

integration.dependencies: glibc (malloc, fopen/fread/fwrite, memset, clock_gettime, printf); Python 3 for verify.py
integration.min_toolchain: GNU as with Intel-syntax AVX2/FMA support (README: binutils 2.40, GCC 12.2.0)
integration.platforms: x86-64 Linux, AVX2 and FMA required
integration.thread_safety: not documented; matrix_mul uses only its arguments and registers (no globals), so separate output matrices can be computed concurrently
integration.drop_in_for_baseline: partial — matrix_mul uses the same Matrix struct layout as the C harness but is a local label; it must be made .global and called with a column count that is a multiple of 8 and at least 8

gotchas: Shipped output does not come from the FMA kernel: the committed output_asm.bin is bit-identical to output_c.bin (0 of 40,000 elements differ) and equals a non-FMA i-k-j recomputation from the committed matrix_a.bin/matrix_b.bin, while an FMA recomputation differs in 13,999 elements (max 2.84e-14, exactly the first README's table). The file was produced by the earlier scalar SSE2 assembly and never regenerated, so `make verify` on the repo's files shows no FMA difference, and the current README's 1.42e-14 figure came from a different random draw (gen_matrix seeds with time(NULL)).

Baseline crippled by build flags: CFLAGS = -O3 -Wall -Wextra -fPIE with no -march, so the README's claim that gcc 'auto-vectorizes with AVX' and emits vmulpd + vaddpd cannot hold; the 1.66x mostly measures 4-wide FMA against 2-wide SSE2. The repo description's '~150% faster' contradicts the README's 1.66x.

The assembly timer passes clock id 0 (CLOCK_REALTIME) although its comments and the README say CLOCK_MONOTONIC (the C side uses CLOCK_MONOTONIC); the first README's numbers were wall-clock only because the original timer call had swapped arguments (fixed in a20dc02). The Makefile ITERS variable is never passed to either program, so the README's `make benchmark ... ITERS=500` example still runs 1,000 iterations.

ABI shortcuts in the assembly: matrix_load, matrix_mul, matrix_save, matrix_create and matrix_free call into libc with a stack misaligned by 8 bytes, main overwrites callee-saved r12-r15 without saving them, and matrix_load ignores fread failures (the C version checks them).
pick_this_over_siblings_when: Rarely: FP-ASM (TACITVS) measures its hand-written kernels against gcc -O3 -march=native and seelabs/nasm against g++ -O3 reference code, so their ratios say more about assembly versus a compiler; pick this only as a minimal AVX2/FMA matmul teaching example, and use a BLAS for actual matrix work.
verified_claims_summary: On an unnamed AVX2/FMA x86-64 CPU (GCC 12.2.0, binutils 2.40), 1,000 multiplications of 200x200 double matrices took a mean 3.043 s for the C i-k-j loop built with -O3 (baseline x86-64, so SSE2) against 1.823 s for the AVX2/FMA assembly over five runs (1.66x, about 2.63 vs 4.39 GFLOP/s); no AVX2/FMA build of the C loop and no BLAS were measured.
status_note: Single-author experiment of four commits on 2026-05-12 with 0 stars and no issues; MIT-licensed and small enough to copy, but it is a demonstration program with a small-matrix correctness bug and a stale committed output file, not a reusable kernel.
